newsitem.title: USA: Citric acid makers pay $94 mln to settle U.S. suit.
newsitem.headline: Citric acid makers pay $94 mln to settle U.S. suit.

text.p: Four companies that make citric acid have agreed to pay $94 million to settle a civil price-fixing suit, a lawyer for the plaintiffs said Monday.
The agreement was filed on Monday in San Francisco with U.S. District Court Judge Fern Smith, who must still approve the proposed settlement, the lawyer, Joseph Cotchett, said.
Under the proposed settlement, Haarmann & Reimer Corp of Springfield, New Jersey, will pay $46 million and Archer Daniels Midland Co will pay $35 million, court documents show.
Hoffman-LaRoche Inc, a subsidiary of Switzerland-based Roche Holding, will pay $5.68 million and Jungbunzlauer Inc of Austria will pay $7.57 million, court documents show.
Litigation will continue against a fifth defendant, Cargill Inc, which did not join the settlement, the court papers show.
The lawsuit accused the five companies of fixing the price of citric acid, a food additive used in a wide range of products. All four companies that settled denied any wrongdoing or liability.

"The proposed settlement agreements with these defendants are a compromise of disputed claims and do not mean that liability or damages would have been found against any of them," a notice of settlement filed with the court said.

The suit was filed last year by food processors in California's San Joaquin Valley, Cotchett said. It was a class-action suit on behalf of all customers who bought citric acid in the United States from any of the defendants between July 1, 1991 and June 30, 1995. "We're very delighted with the settlement as it will return a lot of money to manufacturers across the United States," Cotchett said.
Officials of Cargill, Archer Daniels Midland and Haarmann & Reimer could not immediately be reached for comment.
In October, Archer Daniels Midland said it agreed to plead guilty to two federal counts of price fixing in the sale of agricultural products and to pay record fines totaling $100 million.
Last week, a federal grand jury in Chicago indicted three former top Archer Daniels Midland executives for conspiring to fix prices of the feed additive lysine, the Justice Department said.
